title: 48 hours, 14 days, and your right to speak: the notice rules for Florida condo board meetings
seoTitle: Florida Condo Board Meeting Notice Rules for Owners
description: Florida condo boards must post notice 48 hours ahead, and 14 days for some votes. Here is what a meeting notice must say and what owners can do there.
dek: Your board can't just get together and spend your money. Florida law says when a meeting must be announced, what the notice must say, and what you can do once you walk in.
facebook: Ever found out about a condo board vote after it already happened? Florida law sets the clock: 48 hours' notice for most board meetings, 14 days for some. Here's what the notice must say and what you can do at the meeting.

body.text: Most decisions in a Florida condo are made at board meetings. That is where the budget takes shape, contracts get signed and repairs get approved. So the law gives owners a simple promise: you get told before the board meets, you get told what it plans to discuss, and you can be in the room.

The rules are in section 718.112(2)(c) of the 2026 Florida Statutes, the part of the condo law that covers board meetings. This article explains them in plain words. It is a guide, not legal advice. Your association's own bylaws can add details, and the association attorney is the right person for questions about your building.

body.title: Terms to know
body.text: Board meeting: under the condo law, a gathering of the directors where a quorum of the board is present and association business is discussed. Quorum: the smallest number of directors who must be present for the board to act. Posted conspicuously: put up where owners will see it, at the spot on the condo property the board has chosen by rule. Official records: the papers the association must keep and let owners see. Special assessment: a one-time charge to owners on top of regular monthly or quarterly dues.

For an ordinary board meeting, notice must be "posted conspicuously on the condominium property at least 48 continuous hours before the meeting," except in an emergency. Continuous means the notice stays up the whole time. A note taped up Monday night and taken down Tuesday morning does not count.

The notice must "specifically identify all agenda items." A vague line like "old business" is not enough. The board generally may act only on what is listed. The one exception is an emergency: the board can take up an item that was not on the notice by a vote of at least a majority plus one of the board members. That action must then be noticed and ratified, meaning approved again, at the next regular board meeting.

The board picks where notices are posted, by rule. It may also adopt a rule to post notices on the association's website or on closed-circuit TV, in addition to the posting on the property. If it uses a website, owners with an email address on file must get an electronic notice with a link to it.

Two kinds of decisions need much more warning. If the board will consider a special assessment that is not an emergency, or a change to the rules about how owners may use their units, notice must be mailed, delivered or sent electronically to every owner and posted on the property at least 14 days before the meeting. The person who gives that notice must sign an affidavit, a sworn statement, which is filed among the association's official records.

Any notice for a meeting where regular or special assessments will be considered must say so, and must give the estimated cost and the purpose of the assessment. And if the board plans to approve a contract for goods or services, a copy of the contract must come with the notice or be made available as the statute describes.

Boards may meet by video conference, but the notice must say so. It must include a link and a call-in phone number so owners can join from home, plus the address of a physical place where owners can attend in person. The meeting must be recorded, and the recording is kept as an official record of the association.
Directors themselves may attend by phone or real-time video, according to the state's Division of Condominiums. Those directors count toward the quorum and can vote.
What owners can do at the meeting

items: Attend. Board meetings with a quorum present are open to all unit owners.
Speak. Owners have the right to speak "with reference to all designated agenda items." The board may adopt written, reasonable rules on how often, how long and in what way owners speak.
Record. Owners may record the meeting. The Division of Condominiums says the board can adopt written rules, for example that equipment must not make distracting sound or light.

Ask questions. In residential associations with more than 10 units, the board must meet at least once each quarter, and at least four times a year the agenda must include a chance for owners to ask the board questions.

Add an item. If owners holding 20 percent of the voting interests sign a petition, the board must put the item on the agenda within 60 days, at its next regular meeting or at a special meeting called for it.

body.text: There are limits. Two kinds of meetings do not have to be open: meetings with the association's attorney about proposed or pending lawsuits to get legal advice, and board meetings about personnel matters. Directors may email each other, but they may not vote on association business by email.

Committees count too. A committee that takes final action for the board, or makes recommendations on the budget, follows the same notice rules. Other committees do as well, unless the bylaws exempt them. The Division of Condominiums says owners have the right to attend and observe committee meetings.

items: Find out where your board posts notices. Ask the manager in writing if you don't know.
If the association uses a website or email notices, make sure your current email is on file.
Read the agenda before the meeting. If an assessment is listed, look for the estimated cost and purpose.
Ask for a copy of any contract on the agenda before the vote.
If you think the rules were not followed, write to the board first. You can also contact the state's Division of Condominiums or the Condominium Ombudsman's office for information.

body.text: If you are a board member:

items: Check that your posting rule, and any website or email notice rule, is written down and current.
Before each meeting, ask your manager to confirm the notice went up 48 continuous hours ahead, or 14 days ahead with an affidavit when required.
Make sure every agenda item is listed specifically, and that assessment items show cost and purpose.
For video meetings, confirm the link, phone number, physical address and recording.
When in doubt about an emergency item or a closed session, ask the association attorney before the meeting, not after.

faq.q: How much notice is required for a condo board meeting in Florida?
faq.a: At least 48 continuous hours, posted conspicuously on the condominium property, except in an emergency. Meetings that will consider a nonemergency special assessment or a change to unit-use rules need at least 14 days' notice, mailed, delivered or sent electronically to owners and posted on the property.

faq.q: Can condo owners speak at board meetings in Florida?
faq.a: Yes. Section 718.112(2)(c) gives owners the right to speak on all designated agenda items. The board may adopt written, reasonable rules about how often, how long and in what way owners may speak.

faq.q: Can I record my condo board meeting?
faq.a: Yes. Florida law lets owners record board meetings. The board can adopt written rules about recording, for example that equipment must not make distracting sound or light.

faq.q: Can a Florida condo board vote on something that wasn't on the agenda?
faq.a: Only in an emergency. The item needs a vote of at least a majority plus one of the board members, and the action must be noticed and ratified at the next regular board meeting.

faq.q: Can a condo board hold a closed meeting in Florida?
faq.a: Only in two cases: meetings with the association's attorney about proposed or pending litigation to get legal advice, and board meetings about personnel matters. Other board meetings with a quorum present are open to owners.
